newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Peacekeepers kill wanted Bosnian Serb police chief.
newsitem.headline: Peacekeepers kill wanted Bosnian Serb police chief.

text.p: NATO-led peacekeepers on Thursday shot dead Bosnian Serb police chief Simo Drljaca, who led brutal ethnic cleansing operations against Moslems and Croats in northern Bosnia in 1992.

Drljaca, who headed the police in the northwestern town of Prijedor until last autumn, was killed in self-defence when he fired on soldiers trying to arrest him on war crimes charges, a NATO statement said. A British trooper was slightly wounded.
Prijedor hospital director Milan Kovacevic was arrested in a parallel operation and was to be turned over to the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague for trial.
Although their names were not on the official list of war crimes suspects published by the tribunal, they had been mentioned in sealed indictments, according to a Western official in Sarajevo.
The former Serb mayor of the Croatian town of Vukovar was seized last month under similar circumstances and is now in jail in The Hague.
NATO denied peacekeepers had broken their own ground rules and hunted the men down although the raids, codenamed "Operation Tango", showed every sign of careful planning.
Spokesman Colonel Steven Rausch said they were carried out on "direct orders" from NATO commander General George Joulwan and Secretary General Javier Solana.
Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic claimed Drljaca was shot at his home where he lived openly with NATO's knowledge.
Prijedor police said Kovacevic was arrested at the hospital by four NATO soldiers who allegedly bluffed their way into the building before drawing guns.
According to the police, Drljaca's 17-year-old son and brother-in-law and who were with him have not been seen since.

NATO described the arrest force as multinational but British NATO troops are responsible for the Prijedor sector of northern Bosnia, where thousands of Moslems and Croats were driven from their homes by Drljaca's paramilitary units at the start of the war.
The region was notorious for detention camps such as Omarska and Keraterm, where Moslem and Croat men rounded up by Drljaca's force's were beaten, tortured and killed.

"Operation Tango'" gave teeth to recent warnings by the U.S.-led allies who underwrote the Bosnian peace agreement that they were ready to get tougher with scores war crimes suspects still at liberty in former Yugoslavia.
The most prominent among them are ex-Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic and his wartime army commander General Ratko Mladic, who have both been indicted twice.
Mladic was seen sauntering in a central Belgrade shopping parade on Wednesday and attention has been focused again on Karadzic by his attempts to topple Plavsic this month.
Plavsic, who fears she may have been compromised in Serb eyes by Western support for her battle with Karadzic and his hardliners, condemned Drljaca's killing.

She demanded Kovacevic's release and told peacekeeping commander General William Crouch in a letter that "I fear the reaction of the people will be terrible and I cannot bear any responsibility for this."
The Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA said Drljaca was the first victim on a secret NATO list to liquidate 40 prominent Serbs but did not give other names.
Peacekeeping officials were immediately worried about the danger of retaliaton against their staff on the ground in Bosnian Serb territory.
There are around 100 staff of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in the Bosnian Serb republic and hundreds of international police.
During the war, Bosnian Serbs took U.N. peacekeepers hostage at moments of crisis and on one occasion chained them to targets of possible attack by NATO warplanes.
Drljaca was sacked as Prijedor police chief at the insistence of NATO after he and his men threatened a unit of Czech peacekeepers with banned weapons.
But he was suspected of continuing to be active behind the scenes and of organising the obstruction of efforts to implement the peace process including the return of refugees.
A burly hardliner, he used to boast to journalists at Prijedor police station of his exploits in the early months of the war when a reign of terror gripped northern Bosnia.

Moslem families cowered in their homes as their menfolk were seized by armed Serb patrols in the streets of Prijedor and surrounding towns and villages. The scenes of emaciated prisoners held behind barbed wire at Omarska shocked the world.

Drljaca claimed he was defending the West against Moslem fundamentalism and told one Reuter journalist: "What Europe has done is to cunningly put Serbs again in the position of defending it. See what a whore Europe is."
He brushed aside international condemnation saying: "There's no more messing about, we're digging in."
A Western diplomat said after learning of his death: "He's still going to stand trial but it'll be in a different court."
